No. 25-246
IN THE
Supreme Court of the United States
___________________________________
KENNETH J. JOUPPI,
Peti
tioner,
v.
ALASKA,
Respondent.
___________________________________
ON WRIT OF CERTIORARI TO
THE ALASKA SUPREME COURT
___________________________________
BRIEF OF AMICUS CURIAE
LEGAL ENTERPRISE FOR NEUTRAL
STANDARDS (“LENS”) IN SUPPORT
OF RESPONDENT
___________________________________
Steven Tessler
TESS LAW LLC
2833 Smith Ave., #138
Baltimore, Maryland 21209
(872) 222-7377
steven@tesslaw.org
Counsel for Amicus Curiae
LEGAL PRINTERS  LLC !  Washington, DC! 202-747-2400 ! legalprinters.com

i

QUESTION PRESENTED

Jouppi owned and piloted an aircraft loaded for
a flight to Beaver, a roadless Alaska village that had
voted to prohibit alcohol. Troopers stopped him before
takeoff and found 72 beers, including a six -pack in
plain view. The constitutional ruling rested on his
attempt to transport at least that six-pack. Following
his conviction, Alaska law required forfeiture of the
$95,000 aircraft, although the maximum cash fine for
his offense was $10,000.

The question is: may a court, reviewing an
instrumentality forfeiture for gross dispropor -
tionality, credit the legislature’s assessment of the
harms and the defendant’s actual conduct threatened,
even without a separately identifiable injury and even
when the property’s value exceeds the maximum cash
fine?

ii

TABLE OF CONTENTS
Question Presented ..................................................... i

Table of Authorities .................................................. iii

Interest of Amicus Curiae ........................................... 1

Summary of Argument ............................................... 1

Argument ..................................................................... 2

I.  Jouppi’s alcohol delivery is not harmless, even if
stopped before it reaches its destination, just as a
drunk driver arrested before he kills someone is
not innocent. ......................................................... 3

II.  Attempting to fly alcohol into a dry village is itself
the harm, and the legislature can constitutionally
punish Jouppi for that attempt alone. ................. 6

III. Jouppi’s plane is not immune merely because it
costs more than the maximum fine; a fine and a
forfeiture serve different ends. ............................. 9

Conclusion ................................................................. 11

1

INTEREST OF AMICUS CURIAE1

The Legal Enterprise for Neutral Standards
(“LENS”) is an independent legal research and
appellate advocacy organization. LENS cares about
the rule the Court adopts, not who wins, because that
rule will decide the next case and every one after it.
Clear rules are fair in themselves, even when they
produce a harsh result in a particular case, because
the law should apply the same way to the sympathetic
and the unpopular, the powerful and the weak.

Jouppi’s six-pack and $95,000 airplane make it
easy for most people to take Jouppi’s side. But the way
the narrative is being advanced  does not change the
rule. If courts (and legislators) cannot weigh the harm
a crime threatened before it was completed, a drunk
driver stopped before he hits anyone would be
harmless, and any punishment would be
constitutionally excessive. That cannot be right.
LENS believes governments should be allowed, when
the harms are rational, real, and uncontrived, to
punish the instrumentalities used to cause them.

SUMMARY OF THE ARGUMENT

The Court should hold that a forfeiture may
rest on the harm the defendant’s actual conduct
threatened, even if no one was hurt, and that the
instrumentality’s value alone does not make it
excessive. Jouppi’s attempted delivery did not become

1 No counsel for a party authored this brief in whole or
in part, and no person other than amicus curiae and its counsel
made a monetary contribution intended to fund the preparation
or submission of this brief.

2

harmless merely because troopers stopped his plane.
The Eighth Amendment counts the harm an offense
threatens. Whether a delivery itself into a roadless,
dry village is per se dangerous is a decision for the
legislature, and unless that judgment is wholly
untethered from reality, courts owe it substantial
deference. Jouppi still answers only for what he
actually did, not for what other offenders did. Finally,
forfeiting instrumentalities is common, so the plane’s
value does not matter.

ARGUMENT

Jouppi’s attempted delivery did not become
harmless merely because troopers stopped his plane.
The defendant in Paroline  possessed “between 150
and 300 images of child pornography, two of which
depicted the respondent victim.” Paroline v. United
States, 572 U.S. 434, 441 (2014) . He pleaded guilty
only to “possession of material involving the sexual
exploitation of children,” and no separate loss could
be traced to him, yet the court still found he
contributed to the plaintiff’s continuing injury. Id.  at
441, 456–57. The direct crime was committed only by
the person who originally took the pictures, yet the
law punishes everyone who has or continues to trade
in those pictures. Nor is property which is used to
commit a crime exempt just because it is expensive; a
bank robber who utilizes a $3 million Bugatti as his
getaway car does not have a claim for its return just
because the maximum cash fine applicable for his
crime is less than the vehicle’s total value. He chose
the car, and one who deliberately treads “perilou sly
close to an area of proscribed conduct shall take the

3

risk.” Cf. Boyce Motor Lines, Inc. v. United States, 342
U.S. 337, 340 (1952).

The defendant in Bajakajian willfully failed to
report lawful currency, but he did “not fit into the
class of persons for whom the statute was principally
designed,” so his culpability and the harm he caused
were both “minimal.” United States v. Bajakajian, 524
U.S. 321, 338–39 (1998). His money was “the proceeds
of legal activity” meant “to repay a lawful debt,” and
he could have taken every dollar out of the country
simply by reporting it. Id.  at 337– 38. Jouppi, by
contrast, was a pilot attempting to fly alcohol into a
village that voted to ban it, which is exactly the
conduct the statute targets. App. 24a–26a. Forfeiting
the $95,000 plane he was flying is not grossly
disproportionate to flying alcohol into Beaver in
violation of the statute.

I. Jouppi’s alcohol delivery is not harmless,
even if stopped before it reaches its
destination, just as a drunk driver
arrested before he kills someone is not
innocent.

The Eighth Amendment counts harm
“threatened to the victim or society,” even before
anyone is injured. Solem v. Helm , 463 U.S. 277, 292
(1983). In Paroline, the knowledge that her images
were “circulated far and wide” “renewed the victim’s
trauma,” even though the defendant himself never
touched her. 572 U.S. at 439– 41. The possessor of an
existing image need not commit another physical
assault to sustain the market that “drives production”
or to extend the victim’s injury. Id. at 439–40.

4

The “cause of the victim’s general losses” was
the continuing trade in her images, and the defendant
was “a part of that cause.” Id. at 456. Although no one
could identify “a discrete, readily definable
incremental loss” attributable to him, his
participation in the process causing those losses was
“indisputable.” Id. at 456–57. Each participant helped
in “sustaining and aggravating” the injury. Id. at 457.

The law routinely punishes dangerous conduct
before anyone is “hurt.” Under 21 U.S.C. § 881(a)(4) ,
an aircraft is forfeitable when it is merely “intended
for use” to transport drugs, even if no drugs are ever
delivered, and Congress “understood” that provision
“as serving to deter and to punish.” Austin v. United
States, 509 U.S. 602, 620, 622 (1993) . Likewise, a
commercial pilot who “operates . . . a common carrier
while under the influence of alcohol” faces up to
fifteen years in prison, whether or not he ever crashes.
18 U.S.C. § 342. Three Northwest Airlines pilots
convicted of flying a “commercial passenger airplane”
while drunk “deplaned in Minneapolis” without
incident, yet the Eighth Circuit affirmed their
convictions and the limits on their flying because
their conduct “resulted in a great risk to many lives.”
United States v. Prouse, 945 F.2d 1017, 1020–21, 1026
(8th Cir. 1991).

Possession of enough cocaine to yield 32,500 to
65,000 doses “threatened to cause grave harm to
society.” Harmelin v. Michigan , 501 U.S. 957, 1002
(1991) (Kennedy, J., concurring in part and
concurring in judgment). Alcohol reaches a dry village
the same way drugs reach users, one delivery at a
time. Requiring each delivery to produce its own

5

identifiable injury would render the prohibition null
where it matters most. Alaska’s legislature found that
“the dangers resulting from alcohol abuse are
particularly acute in rural areas of the state because
the communities are small, isolated, without
adequate law enforcement, without adequate health
care facilities, and populated by people who are
closely related and interdependent.” Resp. Br. 10
(quoting 1986 Alaska Sess. Laws ch. 80, § 1(6)).

A related concern is that tolerated violations
can encourage others to disregard the law. Six field
experiments found that observing violations of one
norm or legitimate rule made participants more likely
to violate others. Kees Keizer, Siegwart Lindenberg &
Linda Steg, The Spreading of Disorder, 322 Science
1681, 1681– 85 (2008) . Courts owe substantial
deference here, because “judgments about the
appropriate punishment for an offense belong in the
first instance to the legislature.” Bajakajian, 524 U.S.
at 336.

Jouppi’s shipment needed no audience to do
harm. It would have increased the availability Beaver
voted to restrict, and residents of dry villages
“dramatically benefited from reduced alcohol
availability.” Resp. Br. 10 . That evidence does not
depend on Jouppi inducing anyone else to break the
law.

Cato and the Fines and Fees Justice Center
argue that proportionality must rest on actual
conduct, not “theoretical or potential harms.” Cato &
FFJC Br. 11 . An interrupted attempt is actual
conduct, and its threatened harm does not disappear

6

because police intervene. The harm inquiry may
consider what would have occurred “[h]ad [the] crime
gone undetected.” Bajakajian, 524 U.S. at 339. Here,
had Jouppi’s crime gone undetected, the alcohol
would have landed in Beaver, which is the very
outcome the law prohibits. Take the troopers out of
the picture and change nothing else; all that is left is
the delivery Jouppi was attempting, with no added
conduct, imagined victim, or worst-case result.

II. Attempting to fly alcohol into a dry village
is itself the harm, and the legislature can
constitutionally punish Jouppi for that
attempt alone.

Jouppi is answering for the alcohol he actually
tried to deliver, not for every alcohol- related assault
or death in Alaska; the consequences of that choice
are his alone to bear. Paroline  confirms the limit.
Holding one possessor liable for millions in losses
“collectively caused by thousands of independent
actors” raised a “real question” of excessive
punishment. Paroline, 572 U.S. at 456. The award
therefore had to reflect the defendant’s “relative role
in the causal process” underlying the victim’s losses.
Id. at 458.

In Paroline the Court treated the defendant as
“a part of the overall phenomenon that caused her
general losses,” and not the whole of it. Id. at 456-57.
The same logic applies here. If every participant had
to cause a separate, identifiable injury, harms built
from repeated violations would simply disappear, and
if every participant answered for the whole harm, the
smallest violation could justify the largest sanction.

7

All the court must do is identify the harm the
law targets and connect it to what the defendant did,
i.e., how much he carried, his role, and how he used
his property. PLF warns against “tenuous, remote, or
peripheral” causal links. PLF Br. 8 . Here the link is
anything but remote; Jouppi’s flight would have
added alcohol to the supply Beaver forbade by statute.

Jouppi asks whether national traffic harms
justify forfeiting “every car that goes a mile over the
limit.” Pet. Br. 32. They do not, because the harm a
court weighs is the harm the defendant’s own conduct
threatened in its circumstances, and a mile over th e
limit on an empty highway threatens very little. That
is why States utilize tiered enforcement and bigger
tickets in construction zones and the like, even if no
driver actually injures anyone; the same act can have
different weight in different circumsta nces. Alaska
may likewise weigh the danger of the delivery Jouppi
attempted in Beaver, without waiting for that danger
to become an assault, hospital visit, or death.

Pacific Legal Foundation is correct that
individual culpability matters. PLF Br. 4 –7. It then
describes Jouppi’s conduct as “nonfeasance,” saying
he “failed to discover” the six -pack. Id. at 9 . The
legislature can also  say that failure to perform  the
required due diligence is a punishable failure in and
of itself  if it thinks the crime is severe enough. See
United States v. Balint , 258 U.S. 250, 252– 54 (1922)
(permitting punishment of even unknowing violations
to “stimulate proper care”).

8

In any case, the constitutional ruling concerns
the delivery Jouppi actually attempted. App. 24a–
25a.

Jouppi owned the aircraft, operated the air
service, piloted the flight, knew Beaver was dry, and
had the six -pack in plain view. App. 19a– 27a, 32a–
34a. Nor does the result turn on whether he knew
about any of the beer as the legislature can punish
accidents to “stimulate proper care” if the outcome is
sufficiently severe and it needs to deter. Balint , 258
U.S. at 252–54.

A medical emergency in Beaver arises more
than 100 miles from the nearest hospital, with no
road out of the village. Resp. Br. 12. The consequences
for bringing alcohol into a dry village is a decision for
the legislature, and unless its judgment is wholly
untethered from reality, courts should not involve
themselves by predicting which injury this six -pack
would cause.

Jouppi loaded the aircraft and started its
engine. Resp. Br. 13–14. Troopers, not Jouppi, ended
that flight. Jouppi’s role as the pilot of an actual
alcohol delivery places him within the very class of
actors the forfeiture provision targeted. App. 26a. The
beer Jouppi actually tried to deliver, its destination,
and his aircraft’s use bear on “the gravity of the
defendant’s offense.” Bajakajian, 524 U.S. at 336-37.

Cato and the Fines and Fees Justice Center
also propose a separate inquiry into the offender’s
ability to support himself and his family, and the
Eighth Amendment Scholars trace the historical

9

protection of an offender’s means of subsistence. Cato
& FFJC Br. 10 –11, 14– 18; Eighth Amendment
Scholars Br. 20–22, 25–28.

The Alaska Supreme Court considered the
protection and found that Jouppi had not shown that
forfeiture would deprive him of his livelihood: he was
largely retired, would probably sell the returned
plane, and had another aircraft. App. 26a–27a. Jouppi
also expressly excluded the livelihood issue from his
petition. Cert. Reply Br. 5 n.*.

III. Jouppi’s plane is not immune merely
because it costs more than the maximum
fine; a fine and a forfeiture serve different
ends.

Alaska authorized a $10,000 maximum fine
and forfeiture of Jouppi’s $95,000 aircraft. App. 22a–
23a. The fine does not exhaust the authorized
punishment and what appears at first glance to be an
imbalanced ratio does not per se make the
punishment excessive. This Court has long recognized
that forfeiture may punish more than the fine,
without treating the fine as a ceiling. Forfeiture of a
roughly $1,000 car for a $500-fine offense “can result
in even greater punishment than the criminal
prosecution.” One 1958 Plymouth Sedan v. Com. of
Pa., 380 U.S. 693, 701 (1965). That exclusionary-rule
case recognized additional punishment, above and
beyond the statutorily established limits, not a
constitutional ceiling.

Unlike the currency in Bajakajian , Jouppi’s
aircraft supplied “the actual means by which an

10

offense was committed,” like a car transporting
concealed goods. Bajakajian, 524 U.S. at 333 n.8, 334
n.9. Instrumentalities in particular warrant harsher
punishment because they are enablers of more bad
conduct, they make the offense possible or increase its
reach. Forfeiture serves the law by “preventing
further illicit use of the conveyance.” Calero-Toledo v.
Pearson Yacht Leasing Co. , 416 U.S. 663, 686- 87
(1974). Here, aircrafts are the means by which alcohol
reaches a roadless village, and aircrafts can make
that trip again and again. A cash fine leaves the plane
available for the next flight; forfeiture takes it away
and makes using valuable equipment to offend more
costly.

Drug scales may be seized because they
perform the same unlawful function “whether made
of the purest gold or the basest metal” and bear a
“close enough relationship to the offense.” Austin, 509
U.S. at 627– 28 (Scalia, J., concurring in part and
concurring in judgment). Forfeiting instrumentalities
is common; “a long and unbroken line of cases holds
that an owner’s interest in property may be forfeited
by reason of the use to which the property is put.”
Bennis v. Michigan , 516 U.S. 442, 446 (1996) . It
should not matter that there may be a large gap
between the market value of the instrumentality and
the crime itself; for an instrumentality, “the value of
the property is irrelevant.” Austin , 509 U.S. at 627
(Scalia, J., concurring in part and concurring in
judgment).

None of this exempts the forfeiture from
review. Punitive instrumentality forfeiture still
requires “a proportionality determination.”

11

Bajakajian, 524 U.S. at 333–34. The maximum fine is
“relevant evidence” of gravity, not a cap. Id.  at 339
n.14. Here, Jouppi attempted exactly the delivery the
statute targets, his plane was the means of making it,
and the legislature reasonably judged that delivery
dangerous to a roadless, dry village. So forfeiting that
plane is not grossly disproportionate, it is merely
justice.

CONCLUSION

The judgment of the Alaska Supreme Court
should be affirmed.

October 2026

Respectfully submitted,
